title: The Greatness of Rain
note: This chapter tells the greatness of rain, which by god’s command keeps the world going, and with it righteousness, wealth and pleasure. That explains why it follows the praise of god.

couplets.plain: Because the rain keeps coming, the world keeps going. So rain should be known as ambrosia.
couplets.pm: Because rain goes on without a break, the world endures, so rain is to be understood as the world’s ambrosia. “World” means living beings, who endure by being born without end, always seen in bodies. Those who take ambrosia don’t die, so the rain that keeps the world enduring is to be known by that name.

links.reason: Credits the world’s going on to rain that keeps coming.

links.quote: rain should be known as ambrosia

couplets.plain: Rain makes good food for those who eat, and rain is itself food for them too.
couplets.pm: Rain produces good foods for those who eat, and for those eating them it is food itself, because it is drunk as water. This is said of people but holds for other creatures too. By ending hunger and thirst in this way, rain keeps living beings going.

links.reason: Gives rain the credit for good food, and counts it a food as well.

couplets.plain: If the sky fails, hunger will settle in the wide world of spreading waters and torment it.
couplets.pm: If rain fails when it is needed, hunger settles in the wide world ringed by the sea and afflicts living beings. The sea is mentioned because, though the world has it, it is no help. With no food, beings die of hunger.

links.quote: hunger will settle in the wide world
links.reason: Pictures hunger gripping the whole wide world once the sky fails.

couplets.plain: If the riches called rain run short, farmers will not plough.
couplets.pm: Farmers do no ploughing if the income called rain falls short. This gives the reason why food runs out.

links.quote: If the riches called rain run short
links.reason: Calls rain riches, and shows ploughing stopping when it runs short.

couplets.plain: It is rain that ruins, and rain again that stands by the ruined and lifts them up. All of it is rain.
couplets.pm: By not falling, rain ruins those who live on the earth. Then, by falling, it helps the ruined and raises them as it ruined them. Rain can do all of this. “All” is said because people’s efforts differ, so the ruinings and raisings are many. This tells the power of rain.

couplets.plain: Unless drops fall from the sky, it is hard to see even the head of green grass.
couplets.pm: You see it only if drops fall from the cloud. If they don’t, at that very moment it is hard to see even the tip of green grass. So not even life with one sense remains.

couplets.plain: Even the vast sea would lose its nature, if the clouds took from it and gave nothing back.
couplets.pm: Even the boundless sea loses its nature if the cloud draws from it and doesn’t rain back into it. Losing its nature means that sea creatures aren’t born and gems and the like don’t form. Even the sea, the source of rain, needs rain. These seven couplets say rain is what keeps the world going.

links.quote: Even the vast sea would lose its nature
links.reason: Even the sea needs the round of rain, and would lose its nature if the clouds took and gave nothing back.

couplets.plain: If the sky dries up, festivals and worship will cease here, even for the gods.
couplets.pm: If rain doesn’t fall, even the gods get no worship from people in this world, neither the daily rite nor the festival joined to it. The festival is performed to make up for lapses in the daily rite, so it is named first.

links.quote: festivals and worship will cease here, even for the gods
links.reason: Even worship of the gods and festivals come to a stop under a dry sky.

couplets.plain: If the sky does not give, neither giving nor austerity will remain in the wide world.
couplets.pm: If rain doesn’t fall, the two righteous acts of giving and austerity don’t exist in the wide world. Giving means handing rightly earned wealth to the worthy, gladly. Austerity means cutting down food through vows, so that the mind doesn’t run after the senses. Giving belongs mostly to household life and austerity to renunciation.

links.quote: neither giving nor austerity will remain

couplets.plain: If the world can’t go on without water, then for everyone, conduct can’t go on without rain.
couplets.pm: For people of any rank, worldly life, meaning wealth and pleasure, can’t go on without water. In the same way the unbroken flow of that water can’t go on without rain. Everyone accepts the first, so the second is clear. Some read it that without rain no one’s conduct is complete. These three couplets say rain keeps righteousness, wealth and pleasure going.
couplets.note: ஒழுக்கு can mean conduct or flow. The plain reading takes conduct. He takes the flow of water, and joins “everyone” to the first half.

links.quote: conduct can’t go on without rain

ideaLinks.quote: If the riches called rain run short, farmers will not plough
ideaLinks.reason: Farmers stop ploughing when rain runs short.

ideaLinks.quote: If the sky does not give, neither giving
ideaLinks.reason: Giving will not last in the world once the sky holds back.

ideaLinks.quote: neither giving nor austerity will remain in the wide world
conduct can’t go on without rain
